headline: What the World’s Richest Man Did to the World’s Poorest Children

paragraphs.text: President Trump’s most lethal policy does not involve the Iran war or Ukraine or vaccinations, although all have been tragic mistakes. Rather, the highest death toll, estimated in the hundreds of thousands and still soaring, manifests itself in tiny unmarked graves in impoverished villages around the world.

Elon Musk has continued to insist that “zero” children died after he fed the United States Agency for International Development “into the wood chipper,” so I invited him to join me on an Africa trip. He declined. He apparently doubts that I’d make a great travel buddy, for he has described me as “evil,” but I thought I still owed him an account of what he missed on this trip to South Sudan — and what South Sudanese people want to show him.

“I will take him to where the graves are, for this is the impact of his cuts,” offered Margret Jokudu, who worked with children with H.I.V., many of whom have died for want of medicines that until then were costing the United States less than 12 cents a day. “Maybe he will shed a tear on these graves.”

Evelyn Letio, a leader of the H.I.V.-positive community in South Sudan, told me that people here were immensely grateful for American assistance over the years, adding that she herself was alive because of that help. But now, she said, those gains are becoming undone.
I told her that some Americans wondered why it should be their responsibility to save the lives of people in distant nations like South Sudan. How would she respond to those American critics?

“The money belongs to them,” she acknowledged. “My government should be helping me, but because my government is not helping me, there are many kind Americans who will say this small money should go to South Sudan.”
What would she say to Musk if he showed up?
“I am boiling with anger,” she said. “We are holding him accountable for the many who died. The good things that America built, he is destroying.”

The first place I would take Musk is the village of Halbul in the remote northwest of the country. It used to have an American-funded clinic that was wildly successful in saving lives. I visited it in early 2025, and it made me proud: Villagers thanked me effusively for America’s generosity, and a woman then in labor named her son Nick, simply because I embodied the country that had established the clinic. Villagers said that since the clinic had opened, there had not been a single maternal or infant death in the area.
So I returned to Halbul to see what had happened since Musk’s cuts and Trump’s defunding of the U.N. Population Fund, which had supported the clinic, forced it to close.

“People have died,” said Lual Garang, a villager, and he knows that because his wife was one of them. She was 21, a mother of two, and she delivered at home because there was no other health center nearby. She died in childbirth, along with their baby.
“If this had been open,” he said, gesturing to the now vacant health center, “my wife would have delivered here, and she’d be alive.”

Another villager, Angelina Awich, told me of her 15-year-old daughter, Adeng, who had been pregnant but had received no prenatal care because of the closing of the clinic. Adeng delivered at home, hemorrhaged and bled to death; the baby died as well.
“If the clinic had been open,” Awich told me heavily, “everything would have been fine.”

The most dangerous thing a woman can do in much of the world is to become pregnant. And because Trump slashed aid and defunded the U.N. Population Fund, the leading supplier of birth control, contraception is less available and sex can be lethal.
This is pro-life and pro-family?

Alor Akel, a mother of two in Halbul, told me that because the clinic closed, she tried to give birth at home. But no baby arrived, so while in labor, she set out walking for four hours to a hospital in the city of Aweil. It turned out that she was carrying twins, and both died.
My incomplete count is that at least two women and seven babies died unnecessarily as a result of the shutdown of this one clinic, along with a number of older children and adults.
That toll doesn’t include tragedies that don’t involve deaths.

Abuk Garang told me that she was raped at 13, and her mother and other villagers confirmed that. Susan Ikoki, the midwife who used to run the clinic, told me that she would have immediately given Abuk emergency contraception as well as antibiotics and postexposure prophylaxis to prevent transmission of H.I.V. or other sexually transmitted infections. But without the clinic, Abuk got no help.

So today Abuk is a 14-year-old mom and school dropout. She has symptoms of a sexually transmitted infection and hasn’t been tested for H.I.V. (Test kits for H.I.V. are now in short supply in the field.) The shame of pregnancy has traumatized Abuk, and it’s not clear whether, as a single mom in a conservative society, she can ever marry.

Like most people I talked to, Abuk had never heard of Musk. So I explained to her and her mother that he was the world’s richest man and had led the effort to slash aid to the world’s poorest children. Did Abuk have a message for him?
“I hope the clinic will reopen,” she said softly.

We don’t know how many have died so far as a result of aid cuts. One uncertain estimate from Boston University was 780,000 deaths in the first year, mostly of children. Another study, in The Lancet, estimated that some 3.1 million children under age 5 would die during Trump’s second term because of his aid cuts — equivalent to 88 children dying each hour.

Here in South Sudan, at least 100 health centers are no longer supported. In the village of Gabat, I visited a government clinic that because of aid cuts had no aspirin, no ibuprofen, no hand sanitizer, no soap, no electricity, no running water, no antibiotics and no mosquito nets. Because the staff hadn’t been paid since March, only 10 health workers were present that day, out of a roster of 23 assigned to it.

“When people know that we don’t have drugs, they don’t come anymore,” Mayen Garang, the chief of the clinic, told me. More than 300 patients used to come daily, while now there are perhaps 30, he said. “So of course children die.”

Garang was examining a 6-month-old girl, Adhieu Yak, who had a fever and bacterial pneumonia. Because the clinic had no medicine that could help, he wrote her mother a prescription for medication to buy in the market, but she shook her head. “I have no money,” she lamented. “I can’t afford the medicine.”
At another empty clinic, in the town of Kuom, Simon Ngong, the assistant nurse in charge, recounted to me all the medicines and supplies he lacked and said, “I’m like a soldier without a gun.”
South Sudan’s humanitarian crisis is compounded by the Iran war, which has raised diesel and fertilizer prices.

Steve Roese, the president of Water Is Basic, a nonprofit that trains women to repair wells, said that before the war, it cost $10,000 to take a container of supplies from Uganda to South Sudan. Now it can cost $19,000.
On top of that, a severe drought has destroyed crops across the region, so some people are already eating wild plants to get by.

This means that just when aid is needed most, it is collapsing. The U.N. World Food Program received more than $1 billion in 2022 to help the South Sudanese, but this year it pulled in just $160 million — including only $12 million directly from the United States. So some 380 nutrition sites around the country have suspended services.

I traveled in Northern Bahr el Ghazal State with Action Against Hunger, a well-respected international nonprofit. Aid cuts have slashed its budget for South Sudan by more than half, so it has had to close 38 nutrition centers.

As a result, the group is unable to help some 35,000 children with severe acute malnutrition, according to Heather Stobaugh, the director of research and innovation for Action Against Hunger. She noted that there have been interruptions not only to lifesaving aid but also to the simplest and cheapest interventions, like deworming children, which can cost just 50 cents a year per child. The same is true of vitamin A supplementation, which costs about $2 per child per year and can reduce child deaths in poor countries by up to 24 percent. (Most American kids get vitamin A in foods, including fortified milk and breakfast cereals.) These are some of the best bargains in global health.
“It’s really frustrating,” Stobaugh said. “We have proven, low-cost, simple interventions. And they have been ripped away from us.”

America’s greatest foreign policy success in my lifetime was arguably the PEPFAR program, which under President George W. Bush turned the tide of the AIDS epidemic, saving more than 26 million lives so far. But now under Trump, elements of it are unraveling. One study found that 1,700 H.I.V. treatment sites have closed down worldwide.

In South Sudan, antiretrovirals are still available in hospitals, but the community health workers who once took the medicines to orphans with AIDS were fired. So these children — most of them infected during childbirth and kept alive for years by bipartisan American generosity — were left on their own.

Scovia Abau, a volunteer with AIDS orphans, gave me the names and details of eight of these children who had been receiving antiretrovirals from a single hospital in Juba, South Sudan, who have since died. The youngest was a 6-year-old boy, James Taban.
Pray tell, Elon Musk, how do you expect a 6-year-old AIDS orphan to obtain medicine on his own?
One of those dismissed community health workers is Hellen Kila, who previously helped 40 people with AIDS get their medicines. She knew that some had died, she said, but wasn’t sure how many.

She cited the example of Mary Kujiang. Neighbors found her body with her two small children, both H.I.V.-positive, beside the corpse. Those children were sent off to relatives in a remote part of the country where there is little prospect that they will have access to medicine, Kila said.

In part because she felt she was failing people who had depended on her, Kila tried to hang herself. Her 14-year-old son kicked down the door, held her body up and shouted for neighbors, who came and cut the noose, she and others told me.

Another former community health worker, Agnes Mindra, told me that until the Musk cuts, she was caring for six orphans who had AIDS and 28 mothers with H.I.V. Now three of the children and five of the women have died, she said.
“At first, there were not many deaths, but now it’s increasing,” she told me. “There is more dying now.”

Humanitarian aid is not just a moral issue, for it advances our interests as well as our values. Aid is an inexpensive way to win soft power worldwide, and it is far cheaper to fight diseases like Ebola and tuberculosis in Africa than at home when they spread.

Musk claimed that closing U.S.A.I.D. would save money, but destroying it so abruptly turned out to be extraordinarily costly. Last year I reported on a State Department document indicating it would cost $6.4 billion to close U.S.A.I.D., but the sum keeps going up. The administration has advised Congress that it needs $19 billion to close out U.S.A.I.D. contracts, and even that figure is incomplete.
Meanwhile, until Musk came along, our aid was costing taxpayers just 23 cents for every $100 of gross national income and saved a life approximately once every 10 seconds.

Democrats were rightly critical of the cuts in humanitarian aid. So now that they will control Congress, I’ll keep an eye on whether they push hard to restore humanitarian programs. It’s not essential that U.S.A.I.D. be revived as an independent agency; what matters most is the assistance itself, not the bureaucratic structure.

(If you’re looking for a way to help, I’ve just published my annual holiday giving guide, recommending three outstanding charities, including two that work internationally. Contributions are matched multiple times, so that each $1 donation becomes $3 or $4 in the field. Find out more at kristofimpact.org.)

I fear Americans will think that all this is tragic but behind us and that it’s time to move on. But if you’re a woman whose child is starving because of aid cuts, you can’t move on. If you’ve contracted river blindness and are losing your sight because Washington cut a health program, you can’t move on. If you were raped and can’t get emergency contraception because Trump cut funding for the U.N. Population Fund, the tragedy isn’t behind you.

So I hope we’ll not just deplore this catastrophe and not just regret the ugliness of the world’s richest man devastating the world’s poorest children, but also push for remedies. We can’t reverse every harm, and we can’t save every life, but public pressure can encourage members of Congress in both parties to restore programs in ways that would mean fewer shrieks of grief from bereaved parents and fewer new child-size mounds of earth.
